name: SiteProof – Website Security Reports
author: Verdant Studio

sections.description:
SiteProof checks the basics of your WordPress website and tells you, in plain language, what needs attention, what to do first and what is already in good shape.

Recent checks are saved. You can see what changed since the previous check, and save a report as PDF to show your team, developer or client what was checked and when.

What SiteProof checks

  • Whether updates are available for WordPress, your plugins and your themes
  • Whether plugins you installed were removed from WordPress.org
  • Whether plugins or themes are installed that you do not use
  • Whether your PHP version still receives security updates
  • Whether your website uses HTTPS
  • How many accounts have administrator access, and which administrator accounts are no longer used
  • Whether technical error details are visible to visitors
  • Whether anyone can sign up and get too many permissions
  • Whether a security plugin and a backup plugin are active

What you get

  • A calm overview. One status, at most five recommended actions in order of importance, and a list of what looks good. No long lists of warnings.
  • Clear next steps. Every action explains what is going on and what to do, without technical jargon.
  • Automatic checks. SiteProof checks your website every week. You can also check at any time with “Check now”.
  • History. By default the 52 most recent checks are kept, about a year of weekly checks, so you can see what was resolved and what is new since the previous check.
  • A shareable report. Save any check as a PDF report, including all actions, all results and recent check history.

What SiteProof is not

SiteProof is not a firewall, malware scanner or backup tool, and it does not change your website. It works alongside the security, backup and hosting tools you already use, and tells you whether the basics are in order.

A result of “Good” means no issue was detected by that check. It is not a guarantee that your website cannot be compromised.

Privacy

SiteProof works without an account and sends nothing to its makers. It only contacts WordPress.org, to check for updates, for your PHP version and for removed plugins. What is sent is described under External requests.

What SiteProof stores, in your WordPress database:

  • Check results, including plugin and theme names and versions. By default the 52 most recent checks are kept; developers can change this number.
  • The most recent login date and time of each administrator, to show accounts that are no longer used. Saved checks refer to those accounts by user ID only.
  • Answers from WordPress.org about removed plugins, with the folder names of the plugins asked about, for up to a year after the last request.

No other personal data is stored. The login times and user IDs are never sent anywhere, and reports never include usernames. Reports do include plugin and theme names, so keep that in mind when you share one. Deleting the plugin removes all SiteProof data. SiteProof adds a suggested text to Settings → Privacy that you can use in your privacy policy.

External requests

SiteProof makes one request of its own. For the removed plugins check, it asks api.wordpress.org about plugins that WordPress’s update check gave no answer for. Only the plugin’s folder name is sent, such as “example-plugin”. Your website address is not sent. If all your plugins are listed on WordPress.org, nothing is sent. How the lookup works and how to turn it off.

For the update and PHP version checks, SiteProof uses WordPress’s own standard requests and adds no data to them.

See the WordPress.org privacy policy for how WordPress.org handles what it receives.
sections.installation:
1. In your WordPress dashboard, go to Plugins → Add New Plugin and search for “SiteProof”.
  2. Click Install Now, then Activate.
  3. Go to SiteProof in the menu and click “Run the first check”. If you do not, SiteProof runs its first automatic check within an hour.
sections.faq:
Is SiteProof a security plugin? Do I still need one?

SiteProof does not block attacks or scan for malware, so yes: keep your security plugin, backups and hosting protection. SiteProof gives you an overview of whether the basics are in order and helps you show that they are checked regularly.

How is SiteProof different from Site Health?

Site Health shows a broad technical overview of your website right now, including performance and server settings. SiteProof focuses on security and maintenance, puts the most important actions first, adds checks Site Health does not do (such as inactive administrator accounts and whether a backup plugin is active), and keeps a history of every check so you can show what was checked and when.

How often does SiteProof check my website?

Once a week, automatically, and whenever you click “Check now”. The weekly check uses WordPress’s built-in scheduler, which runs when your website has visitors, so on a very quiet website it can run a little later.

Who can see SiteProof?

Only administrators. On a multisite network, only network administrators.

Why does a check say “not checked yet”?

WordPress does not keep a login history, so SiteProof records administrator logins itself. For an administrator account without a recent login, SiteProof needs 90 days of records before it can say whether the account is still used. The check explains when the result will be available.

What does it mean when a plugin was removed from WordPress.org?

It can no longer be downloaded or updated from there. This happens for a security issue, at the request of its developer or for breaking the rules of WordPress.org, and the reason is not always published. WordPress keeps running the plugin without telling you. Some removals are temporary, so find a replacement or ask your developer before you delete a plugin your website relies on. For a security issue, do this as soon as possible.

“May have been removed” means the plugin has the same folder name as a removed plugin, but a different name. It can be a renamed plugin, or one that was made for your website.

The check cannot find every removal. It skips single-file plugins, plugins without a WordPress.org readme file and plugins that name another update source, and it does not cover themes.

Can I stop plugin names being sent to WordPress.org?

Yes, for the removed plugins check. For one custom plugin, add this line to the header comment of its main file:

Update URI: false

SiteProof then never looks it up, and WordPress.org no longer offers updates for it. WordPress itself still includes the plugin in its own update check.

To switch the whole check off, add this to a small custom plugin. Reports then state that the check is not included.

add_filter( 'siteproof_checks', fn( $checks ) => array_filter( $checks, fn( $check ) => 'removed_plugins' !== $check->get_id() ) );

How do I create a report?

Click “Save report as PDF” on the SiteProof overview, or on any check in History. Your browser’s print window opens, where you choose “Save as PDF”.

Does SiteProof work on WordPress Multisite?

Yes, per site. Each site in the network gets its own checks and history. Because only network administrators can install updates on a multisite network, SiteProof is only visible to network administrators. There is no combined overview of all sites in the network. The check for unused plugins and themes only runs on single sites, because on a network another site may use them. For the same reason, the removed plugins check treats every plugin on a network as in use.

Can developers change the checks?

Yes. Filters let developers add or remove checks, change limits such as the number of administrators, and recognise more security and backup plugins. See the developer documentation.

Changes made with these filters are listed in every report, so readers can see when a report does not use SiteProof’s standard checks.
sections.changelog:
1.2.0: Nov 25, 2026

  • Add: removed plugins check: tells you when a plugin you installed was removed from WordPress.org, so you can replace it
  • Fix: WordPress, plugins and themes are no longer reported as up to date when the update check failed and there was no earlier update information
  • Fix: maintenance and security releases for older WordPress versions are now reported as “Action recommended”, with how to install them
  • Fix: opening a report no longer logs a PHP deprecation notice
  • Fix: the history page now says how many checks are kept, and shows all of them when the limit is raised with the siteproof_snapshot_retention filter
  • Change: when the status is Good, the overview and report now say how many items could not be checked
  • Change: plugin updates now say “No plugin updates found”, and how many plugins have no update information

1.1.0: Nov 17, 2026

  • Add: unused plugins and themes check: listed by name so you can remove the ones you no longer need. Not run on multisite, because another site in the network may use them
  • Change: the status heading now looks the same on the overview and in the report

1.0.0: Nov 12, 2026

  • First release
